rationale: B wins because it keeps its hands mostly inside the evidence box, which is where founders avoid getting burned. Its refusal of "Live shopping isn't dead in America after all" is exactly the discipline A lacks when A asserts a "shutdown-and-retreat cycle of Western live-shopping efforts" without that fact in the update. A also coughs up the headline "worth less than one times revenue it doesn't keep," which is both confused about GMV versus revenue and bad math against a nearly $5B valuation and $3B sales number.
gaps_in_A: "The $3B figure is gross merchandise volume" is asserted before the update proves it; the set later admits the definition still needs to be pinned down.
"shutdown-and-retreat cycle of Western live-shopping efforts" imports market history that was not supplied. Strong angle if sourced; hallucination if not.
"worth less than one times revenue it doesn't keep" is the kind of clever line that gets a founder corrected in public: $5B is not less than one times $3B, and gross sales are not revenue.
The valuation angle is useful, but it overlaps the take-rate problem and needs cleaner math before anyone points it at a financial reporter.
gaps_in_B: "sneakers and phones" are plausible category examples, but the update only says fashion and electronics. Don't decorate facts when the facts are already usable.
"first hard evidence at scale" overclaims. The update gives Whatnot's claimed scale, not the market's first proof point.
"card sellers built the $3B" is not established; the platform started with cards and collectibles, but the current sales mix is undisclosed.

It kills the valuation angle too quickly. "What a $5B valuation says about Whatnot's take rate" is weak, but private-market valuation versus undisclosed net revenue is a real finance lens if the math is handled cleanly.
